summary:
Same-sex conduct has been lawful in Croatia since 1977, and transgender people may serve openly in the armed forces. Hate-crime legislation enumerates both sexual orientation and gender identity. The age of consent was equalised at 14 in 1998 and raised to 15 by the Penal Code that took effect on 1 January 2013.

Enforcement lags the statute book. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report records that minority representatives describe anti-discrimination provisions covering employment, housing, education and health as inconsistently enforced, that NGOs report uneven judicial handling of discrimination cases and limited access to justice, and that victims are reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and of being victimised during trial. Hate-crime investigations are flagged as inadequate. A 2018 Zagreb Pride report documenting Croatia's implementation of Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 records under-reporting of homophobic and transphobic crimes alongside compiled hate-crime data and case studies, and examines hate speech and freedom of assembly. A 2024 European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination, covering 2023, assesses the transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds.

Legal gender recognition rests on a 2013 legislative amendment that permits registration of a changed gender marker without requiring alteration of sex characteristics. A 2026 article in the Croatian legal journal Elektronicki zbornik radova Veleucilista u Sibeniku works through how police, customs and court officers must conduct searches of trans and gender-nonconforming people under the Criminal Procedure Act, the Police Powers Act, the Customs Act and the law on prison sentences, using case studies of the difficulties that arise in practice. In 2023 the opposition Mozemo! party proposed easier legal gender change and broader IVF access; neither bill had passed as of January 2024.

Registered life partnerships have been available since 2014. A constitutional referendum in 2013 barred same-sex marriage, and family rights have been won mainly through litigation. The Constitutional Court ruled on 7 February 2020 that excluding same-sex couples from foster care was unconstitutional and discriminatory. Mladen Kozic and Ivo Segota became the country's first same-sex foster parents in September 2020 after a three-year legal battle, having twice been rejected by the Center for Social Welfare. Full adoption rights were confirmed by a final court ruling in 2022, and as of January 2024 no national statute regulates same-sex adoption, so the protections in force derive from court rulings. Partner-guardianship, granting permanent parental rights to a non-biological life partner, was first recognised in July 2015.

Article 68 of the Life Partnership Act gives life partners the same health insurance and healthcare rights as married heterosexual couples and prohibits adverse treatment of life partnerships in those areas. Reproductive care is not equal: the Medically Supported Fertilisation Law limits IVF to married heterosexual couples and single infertile women, excluding same-sex couples, and a 2012 law had already allowed single women but not lesbian couples.

Official hostility is documented. A Croatian Parliament session on 'Gender Ideology' featured speakers spreading misinformation about gender, with no LGBTI organisations invited. In 2024 a Zadar prosecutor charged a man for refusing a gay couple's accommodation booking, an incident dating from 2018. The first Pula Pride march was disrupted the day before it took place.

Pride events are held in Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac and Pula, and the Balkans Trans Inter March is among them. Community infrastructure includes three LGBT centres. The first is in Zagreb; a second opened in Split on 24 May 2014, the first in Dalmatia, run by the association Risp-et and presented a month before the fourth Split Pride on 7 June 2014 with mayor Ivo Baldasar attending; a third, LGBTIQ+ Druga Rijeka, was presented in Rijeka in October 2014 with the public backing of mayor Vojko Obersnel and cultural institutions. The Split centre's organisers demanded equal treatment of same-sex families, including marriage and joint adoption, and said institutions create second-class citizens.

Zagreb has the largest gay scene, with clubs, bars and Queer Zagreb programming; venues and beaches described as gay-friendly are also noted in Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik. A commercial travel guide cautions that public displays of affection may draw unwelcome responses in less populated cities and that dedicated venues remain scarce outside Zagreb, though new venues have opened in Split, Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik.
tangentialFactors:
In March 2014 Croatia granted asylum for the first time to a person persecuted on the basis of sexual orientation, a young man who had fled Uganda under the Anti-homosexuality Act.

A Eurobarometer-style survey found that 64 per cent of Croatians agreed school lessons should include information about sexual orientation diversity and 63 per cent about gender identity.
localsOnly:
The blood transfusion institute's rules effectively bar gay and bisexual men from donating blood indefinitely. A 2007 bylaw places men who have sex with men in categories of permanent rejection, and as of 2021 this is framed as 'behaviors or activities that expose them to risk of contracting blood-borne infectious diseases'.

In 2009 the European Committee on Social Rights found that discriminatory statements in a mandatory Croatian school biology textbook violated the European Social Charter. On 1 March 2013 the Minister for Science, Education and Sports announced an action to strip homophobic content from elementary and high school books, especially religious education texts.

A 2016 study examined the psychosocial adaptation and experiences of stigmatisation of children in LGBT families.

Community resources for residents include Zagreb Pride's 2016 guide 'We Have a Family!' for LGBT parents and the 2018 picture book 'My Rainbow Family' for preschool-age children with same-sex parents; the first 500 copies were free with French Embassy funding, and a crowdfunded reprint raised over 7,000 dollars.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents Croatian visa rules, passport gender-marker policy, or entry and border procedures for transgender travellers. The available country coverage is silent on these points, and the position for a trans visitor arriving at a Croatian border is not sourced here.

As of January 2024 no national law regulated same-sex adoption; the rights in force rest on court rulings rather than statute, and the legislative position after that date is not sourced.

The two 2023 opposition bills on legal gender change and IVF access had not passed as of January 2024. Whether either has since advanced is not established by the inventory.

Recorded hate-crime figures for Croatia are affected by documented under-reporting, so the compiled data understate the number of incidents.
